citeAs: Singh, A., Natarajan, V., Shah, M., Jiang, Y., Chen, X., Batra, D., Parikh, D., & Rohrbach, M. (2019). Towards VQA Models That Can Read. arXiv.
creator: Amanpreet Singh, Vivek Natarajan, Meet Shah, Yu Jiang, Xinlei Chen, Dhruv Batra, Devi Parikh, Marcus Rohrbach (Facebook AI Research, Georgia Institute of Technology)
description: TextVQA is a visual question answering dataset of 45,336 questions on 28,408 images that require reading and reasoning about text in images to answer. The images are drawn from Open Images, and each question-image pair has 10 human-provided ground truth answers.
name: TextVQA
rai:annotationsPerItem: 10 answers were collected for each question-image pair; additionally, 1-2 questions were collected per image.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper reports agreement statistics for answers: all 10 annotators agree on the most common answer for 22.8% of questions, while 3 or more annotators agree on the most common answer for 97.9% of questions. Quality control also removed questions where a majority of workers flagged issues such as no text, not a question, not requiring reading, or being unanswerable.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset was collected in a three-stage crowdsourcing pipeline. First, annotators identified images that contained text. Second, annotators wrote 1-2 questions per image that required reading text in the image to answer; for the first question they were instructed to ensure answering required reading the text, and for the second they were shown the first question and asked for a different question with a different answer. Third, following VQA and VizWiz-style instructions, 10 answers were collected for each question. Questions were removed when a majority of workers flagged them as having no text, not being a question, not requiring reading, or being unanswerable, and handcrafted gold questions were used to filter bad annotators.
rai:dataBiases: The paper motivates TextVQA as addressing a gap in existing VQA datasets, where questions requiring reading are infrequent because those datasets were not collected in settings that mimic visually impaired users. It also notes that the majority answer "yes" accounts for only 4.71% of the dataset and yes/no majority-answer questions make up only 5.55%, indicating an intentional design to reduce simple answer bias.
rai:dataCollection: The authors sampled images from Open Images v3, focusing on categories likely to contain text. To identify such categories, they ran the Rosetta OCR system on up to 100 random images per category, computed the average number of OCR boxes, normalized these averages into per-category weights, and sampled images accordingly. They then used a three-stage crowdsourcing pipeline to filter images without text, collect questions requiring reading text, and collect answers.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The source data are images from the Open Images v3 dataset, especially categories that tend to contain text such as billboard, traffic sign, and whiteboard.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes that some images yield zero OCR tokens because the OCR system fails to detect text, even though the images do contain text. It also notes that 8.9% of TextVQA questions can only be answered by combining multiple OCR tokens, which the presented model cannot do. More broadly, the dataset is designed around text in natural scenes and depends in part on OCR quality.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: To target images likely to contain text, the authors ran Rosetta OCR on sampled images from each Open Images category, computed the average number of OCR boxes per category, normalized these into sampling weights, and sampled images using those weights. The final dataset was also filtered by removing images without text, noisy annotator data, and questions flagged by a majority of workers as invalid or unanswerable.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended to facilitate research on visual question answering models that can read and reason about text in natural images, and to benchmark progress on questions relevant to assistive applications for visually impaired users.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Rosetta OCR was used to identify categories likely to contain text during image sampling and to analyze OCR tokens in the dataset.
